title: A backslash in an http(s) URL is silently treated as a forward slash by the browser's URL parser, but not by Python
assumption: A URL parser only treats "/" as a path separator, so a backslash in a URL string stays part of the host or path text it was written in.

input.description: A URL built by concatenating a trusted base domain with user-controlled text that includes a backslash - deliberately, as an SSRF or open-redirect bypass attempt, or accidentally, from a Windows-style path pasted into a URL field.

what_goes_wrong: The WHATWG `URL` parser (used by every modern browser and by Node's global `URL`) treats the backslash exactly like a forward slash for `http`/`https` URLs, splitting the host at it: `new URL("http://example.com\\evil.com/path").hostname` is `"example.com"` with pathname `"/evil.com/path"`. Python's `urllib.parse.urlparse` does not special-case backslashes at all, so it keeps `"example.com\\evil.com"` as one literal hostname string. The same input string resolves to a completely different host depending on which parser read it - a host-based allowlist check written against one parser's output can disagree with the HTTP client (or browser) that actually makes the request using the other's interpretation.
why: The WHATWG URL Standard treats `\` as equivalent to `/` only for "special" schemes (http, https, ws, wss, ftp, file), recording it as a validation error but continuing, because browsers historically normalized backslashes for compatibility with sloppy real-world URLs. For a non-special scheme the backslash is not a separator: `new URL("foo://example.com/a\\b").pathname` keeps it as `/a\\b`. Python's `urllib.parse` follows the RFC 3986 generic syntax, in which a backslash is not a legal URI character at all - but `urlparse` does no character validation, so it simply leaves the backslash inside whatever component it lands in. Neither parser is misbehaving by its own spec; they just answer "what host is this?" differently for the same string.
affects: python (as the disagreeing side: urllib.parse keeps the backslash in the host)

repros.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse
u = urlparse("http://example.com\\evil.com/path")
print(u.hostname, u.path)

fix: Never build a trust decision (an SSRF allowlist, a same-origin check) against a hostname string parsed by one library if the request will actually be issued by a different URL-parsing implementation (a browser, a different HTTP client, another language's service). Normalize backslashes to forward slashes (or reject URLs containing them) before any parsing happens, consistently across every component that will touch the URL.

sources.title: WHATWG URL Standard: special schemes and path-segment separators

test_cases.note: their_extract_hostname(url) must be checked against the SAME parser that will actually dereference the URL - a hostname check written against one URL parser can be bypassed by a client that resolves backslashes differently.
